record.original_question: List all integer solutions to x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 3, or prove that this equation has infinitely many integer solutions.

evidence.quote: Problem 4. Given a Diophantine equation, either list all its integer solutions, or prove that there are infinitely many of them.
The smallest open symmetric equation is x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 3 (22) of size H = 27.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the Diophantine equation
    x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 3
in integers x, y, z ∈ ℤ. Two families of integer solutions are known: (x,y,z) = (1,1,1) and (x,y,z) = (4,4,-5) together with its permutations and the permutations of (4,-5,4), (-5,4,4). Determine whether the set of all integer solutions to this equation is finite or infinite. Specifically, either (a) prove that the only integer solutions are those listed above (and produce a complete list), or (b) prove that the equation admits infinitely many integer solutions.
artifact.status_search_result: The equation x^3+y^3+z^3=3 is a famous open case in the sums-of-three-cubes problem. Only the solutions (1,1,1) and (4,4,-5) (with permutations) are known, and it is not known whether any others exist or whether infinitely many solutions exist. Heuristics (e.g., Heath-Brown) suggest infinitely many solutions, but no proof is known, and extensive computer searches by Booker, Sutherland and others have not found any further solutions.

status_evidence.title: Sums of three cubes — Andrew Sutherland (MIT)
status_evidence.snippet: Survey on x^3+y^3+z^3=k including the still-open case k=3 where only (1,1,1) and (4,4,-5) are known.
status_evidence.claim: The case k=3 remains open: no third primitive solution has been found despite extensive search.

status_evidence.title: Known families of integer solutions of x^3+y^3+z^3=n — Eric Rowland
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses known parametric and sporadic solutions for sums of three cubes equal to n.
status_evidence.claim: For n=3 only sporadic small solutions are known and no parametric family is established.
